extracted.intended_audience: members of Parliament, lawmakers, and the literate public concerned with book licensing and censorship
extracted.subtask_description: A 17th-century polemic arguing against prior licensing/censorship of books, giving principles for when books should be allowed, how readers and licensers should behave, and why licensing is impractical or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against_prior_licensing_as_unlawful
rubrics_metrics.description: Licensing of books (prior restraint/imprimatur) is not derived from any ancient state, polity, Church, or statute but originates from inquisitorial, tyrannous practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton traces the invention and origin of book-licensing to the 'most antichristian Councel' and the Inquisition, arguing that because no well-instituted state used prior licensing historically, the practice is suspect and illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free_admission_of_books_except_monsters
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'issue of the brain' should be admitted freely into the world as births are; only if a book 'prov'd a Monster' (i.e., flagrantly pernicious) might it justly be burnt or destroyed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton allows for extreme, manifestly monstrous cases where destruction is warranted, but rejects prior public trial and suppression as the normal rule; post-public condemnation of clearly monstrous works is distinct from general prior licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: No_pre-publication_judgment_of_books
rubrics_metrics.description: Books should not 'stand before a Jury ere it be borne to the World' undergoing pre-publication judgment by licensers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-publication tribunals imposing judgment is described as a novel and tyrannous practice; Milton stresses that this prior trial of books was never heard of before such inquisitorial systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom_to_read_and_personal_judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should be free to 'Read any books whatsoever' because each person is 'sufficient both to judge aright and to examine each matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites historical/religious precedents (Dionysius Alexandrinus, Eusebius, the Apostle's admonition 'Prove all things') to support the claim that individuals can and should evaluate books themselves rather than rely on prior censorship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposure_to_error_is_necessary_for_virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge and survey of vice (access to books about or containing error) is necessary to constitute and confirm human virtue; seeing vice allows one to abstain and better practice virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues that a 'blank virtue' that has never encountered vice is untested; literary examples (Spencer's Guion) show virtue strengthened by encountering temptations. Thus forbidding all books of vice would remove necessary material for moral growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing_is_ineffective_and_unworkable
rubrics_metrics.description: The licensing order 'conduces nothing to the end for which it was fram'd' and is practically ineffective — scandalous writs and libels continue to be printed and dispersed despite licensing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton notes recurring publication of seditious material despite licensers, arguing enforcement and practical efficacy are lacking and that licensing will be 'vain and frustrat' unless extended into an impossible regime modeled on Trent/Seville.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications_of_licensers
rubrics_metrics.description: A person appointed to judge the birth or death of books 'had need to be a man above the common measure both studious, learned, and judicious'; otherwise mistakes in censure will be grave injustices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton emphasizes the heavy burden such readers would face (tedious, unpleasing, loss of time) and warns that, given the difficulty, future licensers will be ignorant, remiss, imperious, or corrupt (pecuniary), producing poor censorship decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing_slippery_slope_to_total_regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the state undertakes licensing of books it will necessarily be pulled toward licensing other entertainments and private behaviours (music, dances, songs, windows, garments, instruments, village pastimes), making society ridiculous and weary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton uses hypothetical extension of licencing — regulating lutes, violins, ballads, garments, household behaviours — to show the impractical and totalizing consequences of starting with books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer_education_over_coercive_law
rubrics_metrics.description: Unwritten laws of virtuous education, religious and civil nurture, and persuasion are preferable instruments to restrain vice than coercive licensing and legal compulsion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues that moral formation and good education will be more effective than legal prohibitions; law should discern where restraint/punishment is needed and where persuasion suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nuanced_treatment_of_mixed_books
rubrics_metrics.description: Books that are 'partly useful and excellent, partly culpable and pernicious' call for expurgation/expunction and cataloguing rather than simple wholesale prohibition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To implement licensing strictly would create the need for lists of condemned works, careful overseers, expurgators, and catalogs of offending printers — a vast, expensive, and imperfect bureaucracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't_deprive_the_wise_for_fools_sake
rubrics_metrics.description: We should not deprive wise men of advantages to their wisdom merely to restrain fools; a wise man will make use of even idle pamphlets better than a fool will of sacred Scripture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton argues that censorship that limits all readers harms the learned disproportionately and is unjustified because folly cannot be prevented simply by withholding books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_formalistic_language_requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Requiring Latin phrasing (Roman imprimatur) or other formalistic trappings to confer authority on licences is an affectation rooted in Romanizing imitation and not necessary for legitimate regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton ridicules the practice of setting the command in Latin as if no vulgar tongue were worthy to express such presumption, implying licensing should not rest on linguistic formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary_burning_vs_state_prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Private, voluntary acts of burning guilty men's own books (e.g., Ephesians' books by converts) are different from magistrate-imposed prohibition; such private remorse is not a model for public legal prescription.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton distinguishes private voluntary renunciation of corrupt books (which may be imitated voluntarily) from state enforcement, which would be a public imposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial_religious_books_more_dangerous_to_learned
rubrics_metrics.description: Books of religious controversy are 'more doubtfull; and dangerous to the learned then to the ignorant' because they require a guide; ignorant readers seldom are seduced without clerical mediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton notes that controversial tracts need interpretation and teachers, and that many clerics themselves have been corrupted by studying such materials (e.g., Jesuit/Sorbonist comments). This complicates the case for prior banning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical_burden_on_licensers
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of perpetual reading and censoring of all submissions is an intolerable, tedious, and time-consuming imposition on any suitably learned person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton observes the real-world sign that current licensers are already weary, making excuses and wishing to be rid of the office — prognosticating that future holders will be remiss or venal, undermining the system's integrity.
